title: Set a Learning Goal You Can Test
body:
Setting a learning goal you can test means stating what you will be able to do when the learning is done, and how you will prove it, so progress is visible instead of a vague feeling of having studied.

Method. First, name the skill in a sentence. Second, name a task that proves the skill, such as solving a set of problems, building a small item, or explaining the topic without notes. Third, set a date for the first test. Fourth, write the goal down where you will see it. Fifth, test on that date and record the result, pass or not.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for set a learning goal you can test. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: goal: solve 10 fraction problems correctly; proof tasks: 3; test date set: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use testable goals for every self-directed project. Do not use a goal such as study more, because it cannot be tested and therefore cannot be finished, and do not move the test date without recording why. title: Break a Skill Into Parts
body:
Breaking a skill into parts means splitting a large skill into smaller sub-skills that can each be practised and tested alone, so a learner works on one weakness at a time instead of facing the whole skill at once.

Method. First, list the parts of the skill in order. Second, mark which parts are already strong and which are weak. Third, practise the weakest part first, in short sessions. Fourth, test each part alone before combining them. Fifth, combine the parts only after each part passes its own test.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for break a skill into parts. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: parts: 4; weak part: choose the method; practice order: weakest first Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use part-breaking for any skill that feels overwhelming. Do not practise only the parts you already enjoy, because the weak parts are the ones that limit the whole skill, and do not combine parts before each part is sound. title: Choose Resources That Fit the Goal
body:
Choosing resources that fit the goal means matching each learning resource to the part of the skill it must teach, and checking its level, its examples, and its practice tasks before committing weeks to it.

Method. First, list the parts that need resources. Second, for each part, find one resource at the right level, not too easy and not far ahead. Third, check that it includes worked examples and practice tasks, not only explanations. Fourth, try the first section and test whether you can do its tasks. Fifth, keep the resource only if that trial succeeds.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for choose resources that fit the goal. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use resource-fit checks before starting a long course or book. Do not collect many resources for the same part, because unused resources become clutter, and do not keep a resource that teaches a different level than the part you need. title: Make a Study Plan That Fits Your Week
body:
Making a study plan that fits your week means assigning real hours from real days to real parts of the skill, so the plan survives contact with work, family, and rest instead of collapsing in its first week.

Method. First, count the hours actually free in a normal week. Second, assign most of them to the weakest part, and the rest to review. Third, place sessions on named days and times. Fourth, include a rest day and a review session. Fifth, at the end of the week, compare planned hours with actual hours and adjust the next week, not the goal.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for make a study plan that fits your week. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: free hours: 6; planned: 6; plan fits: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use a weekly plan for every ongoing project. Do not plan more hours than a normal week actually holds, and do not plan seven study days, because a plan with no rest is a plan that will be abandoned. title: Learn by Doing a First Small Project
body:
Learning by doing a first small project means using the skill to make something small and complete, early, so mistakes surface while they are still cheap and the learner has proof that the skill works in the real world.

Method. First, choose the smallest complete version of the real task. Second, list its steps before starting. Third, do it, noting every point where you get stuck. Fourth, fix the stuck points by returning to the relevant part. Fifth, keep the finished project as the first entry in a portfolio.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for learn by doing a first small project. Use and limits. Use a first project as soon as the basics of each part are in place. Do not wait until you feel fully ready, because readiness without practice is a feeling, not evidence, and do not choose a first project so large that it cannot be finished. title: Use Spaced Repetition for Remembering
body:
Using spaced repetition for remembering means reviewing material at growing intervals, just before it would be forgotten, so each review strengthens the memory more than the last and total study time falls.

Method. First, turn the material into short testable items, such as questions with answers. Second, review new items after one day. Third, review items answered correctly after longer gaps, such as three days, then seven, then fourteen, then thirty. Fourth, return any missed item to the short gap. Fifth, keep the daily review pile small enough to finish every day.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for use spaced repetition for remembering. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: review gaps in days: [1, 3, 7, 14, 30]; reviews per item: 5; last gap: 30 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use spaced repetition for facts, vocabulary, procedures, and anything that must be recalled without notes. Do not review everything every day, because that wastes the benefit of spacing, and do not skip a scheduled review without rescheduling it. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Get Feedback Without a Teacher
body:
Getting feedback without a teacher means building checks into practice itself: worked answers to compare against, a checklist for your own work, a peer who will look at it, or a real test the work must pass, so errors are found by the work rather than by authority.

Method. First, find a worked answer or a standard to compare against. Second, write a checklist of common errors for this skill. Third, check your own work against both before calling it done. Fourth, ask a peer or a community to look at the finished piece. Fifth, record every error found and practise the part that produced it.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for get feedback without a teacher. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: feedback checks: 4; checks used: worked answer, error checklist, peer look, real test Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use self-feedback for every practice session. Do not call work finished without a check, and do not treat a single peer comment as a final verdict; feedback is evidence to weigh, not a grade to obey. title: Keep an Error Log and Learn From It
body:
Keeping an error log and learning from it means writing down each mistake, what caused it, and what will change next time, so the same mistake stops returning and practice targets real weaknesses instead of comfortable strengths.

Method. First, after each practice session, list the errors made. Second, sort them by cause: misunderstanding, carelessness, or missing knowledge. Third, count which cause appears most. Fourth, practise the part behind the most common cause. Fifth, re-test that part and record whether the error rate fell.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for keep an error log and learn from it. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: carelessness : 1; missing knowledge : 1; misunderstanding : 3; most common: misunderstanding Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use an error log for skills where the same mistakes recur. Do not write errors down without sorting them, because an unsorted list does not show what to practise, and do not hide errors from the log out of embarrassment; the log is private and its purpose is progress. title: Test Yourself Before You Feel Ready
body:
Testing yourself before you feel ready means recalling material from memory, without notes, as the main form of practice, because recall itself strengthens memory far more than re-reading, and a test reveals gaps while there is still time to fix them.

Method. First, close the book or notes. Second, write or say everything you remember about the topic. Third, open the notes and mark what was missing or wrong. Fourth, practise only the missing parts. Fifth, test again after a gap, and compare the two results.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for test yourself before you feel ready. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: first test: 6 / 10; second test: 9 / 10; improvement: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use self-testing for every topic that must be remembered. Do not re-read as a substitute for recall, because re-reading feels fluent while leaving memory untested, and do not test only the parts you already know. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Keep a Learning Journal
body:
Keeping a learning journal means writing a short entry after each session: what was practised, what was learned, what was hard, and what comes next, so the learner can see progress over weeks and pick up exactly where the last session ended.

Method. First, date each entry. Second, write what was practised in one line. Third, write what was learned in one line. Fourth, write what was hard and what will be practised next. Fifth, re-read the last entry before the next session starts.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for keep a learning journal. title: When You Are Stuck, Change the Step
body:
When you are stuck, changing the step means shrinking the task, changing the angle, or finding a worked example, rather than repeating the same failed attempt, because a stuck learner usually needs a smaller step, not more effort on the same step.

Method. First, name exactly where you are stuck, in one sentence. Second, make the task smaller until one step is doable. Third, try a different angle: a diagram, an example, or a concrete case. Fourth, look at a worked example and cover its steps one at a time. Fifth, if still stuck, ask a specific question about the stuck step, not a general request for help.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for when you are stuck, change the step. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: stuck at: choosing the method; smaller steps: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use stuck-step changes whenever progress stops for more than a short session. Do not repeat a failed attempt unchanged, and do not abandon the whole project because one step is stuck; the step, not the project, is the problem. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Teach It Back to Check Understanding
body:
Teaching it back to check understanding means explaining the topic in plain words, without notes, to another person or to an empty chair, because an explanation that cannot be given plainly reveals exactly which part is still unclear.

Method. First, explain the topic from memory, in order. Second, note every point where the explanation stalls or becomes vague. Third, return to the material for exactly those points. Fourth, explain again, and check whether the stall points are gone. Fifth, write the final explanation down as a summary for later review.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for teach it back to check understanding. Use and limits. Use teach-back for any topic that must be understood, not only remembered. Do not read the explanation from notes and call it teach-back, because reading hides the gaps that speaking reveals. title: Build a Portfolio of Finished Work
body:
Building a portfolio of finished work means keeping the best finished pieces from a learning project together, with a note on each about what it proves, so progress can be shown, reviewed, and built on instead of disappearing into scattered practice.

Method. First, keep every finished project, not only the best. Second, choose the pieces that show different parts of the skill. Third, write one line on each piece about what it proves. Fourth, order the pieces from earliest to latest so growth is visible. Fifth, review the portfolio when choosing the next goal.

title: Review and Revise Your Plan Monthly
body:
Reviewing and revising your plan monthly means comparing what was planned with what was actually done, keeping what worked, changing what did not, and setting the next month's goal from evidence rather than from hope.

Method. First, list last month's planned hours and topics. Second, list the actual hours and topics completed. Third, note which parts improved on their tests and which did not. Fourth, keep the methods that produced improvement and replace the ones that did not. Fifth, set next month's goal and hours from that evidence.

title: Learn With Others: Study Partners and Groups
body:
Learning with others means using study partners and groups for the things a lone learner cannot easily supply: questions from another angle, a deadline that is shared, and a listener for a teach-back, while keeping the group's work focused on practice rather than on talk about practice.

Method. First, agree on a shared goal and a regular meeting time. Second, assign each meeting a task to complete together, not a topic to discuss vaguely. Third, take turns explaining and questioning. Fourth, end each meeting by setting the next task and its test. Fifth, leave a group that stops producing practice, politely and without delay.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for learn with others: study partners and groups. Use and limits. Use groups for explanation, questioning, and shared deadlines. Do not use a group as a substitute for solo practice, because the group cannot practise for you, and do not let a group drift into general discussion when its task is unfinished. title: Keep Going: Habits, Plateaus, and Finishing
body:
Keeping going means protecting the habit through plateaus, when visible progress stops for a while, by keeping sessions short and regular, varying practice, and finishing the project rather than starting a new one at the first sign of difficulty.

Method. First, fix a minimum daily session that can be kept even on a bad day. Second, track the streak of days kept, not only the results. Third, when a plateau arrives, vary the practice type before judging the method a failure. Fourth, set a finish line for the current project and cross it before starting the next. Fifth, celebrate finishing by recording the finished work in the portfolio.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for keep going: habits, plateaus, and finishing. Use and limits. Use habit protection for every long project. Do not judge a method during a plateau, because plateaus are a normal part of learning, and do not abandon a nearly finished project for a new beginning, because finishing is itself a skill.
